facts_and_myths.explanation: Clinical studies prove wounds heal up to 50% faster with less scarring under a clean adhesive bandage because cells regenerate best in a moist environment.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Scabs force new skin cells to burrow underneath the dry crust, slowing closure and increasing scar formation.

facts_and_myths.claim: The adhesive bandage was invented by a husband whose wife repeatedly cut herself cooking.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Earle Dickson, a cotton buyer at Johnson & Johnson, invented the ready-to-use Band-Aid in 1920 so his wife Josephine could dress her kitchen burns and cuts independently.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Johnson & Johnson gave Dickson a vice presidency in honor of his worldwide breakthrough invention.

name: Mercury Clinical Thermometer
visual_anchor: A slender triangular glass clinical thermometer showing a silver thread of mercury resting at 37 degrees Celsius against black graduation lines, 9:16 vertical macro.
core_traits: Glass capillary instrument used to measure human body temperature orally or under the armpit
Contains liquid mercury or non-toxic gallium alloy that expands uniformly up a narrow calibrated stem
Features a microscopic constriction above the bulb that prevents the liquid column from dropping until shaken down
Calibrated across the clinical human fever range from roughly 35 to 42 degrees Celsius

facts_and_myths.claim: Normal human body temperature is strictly 37.0 degrees Celsius (98.6 degrees Fahrenheit) for every healthy individual at all times.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Healthy body temperature fluctuates between 36.1 and 37.2 degrees throughout the day due to circadian rhythms, physical activity, and hormonal shifts.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: German physician Carl Wunderlich established the 37-degree standard in 1868 after analyzing 25,000 patients.

facts_and_myths.claim: A clinical glass thermometer must be vigorously shaken downward to reset the liquid column.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The narrow constriction traps the mercury at maximum recorded temperature; centrifugal force from shaking overcomes capillary tension to return liquid to the bulb.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Due to toxic mercury spill hazards, many schools and hospitals have replaced mercury thermometers with alcohol or digital thermistors.

name: Medical Syringe
visual_anchor: A clear plastic medical syringe with precise milliliter markings and a rubber plunger head, reflecting clean clinic light, 9:16 vertical view.
core_traits: Simple reciprocating pump consisting of a tight-fitting plunger sliding inside a calibrated cylindrical barrel
Draws in or expels liquids through an orifice or attached hollow hypodermic needle
Constructed from sterile polypropylene plastic for single-use medical hygiene
Used by school nurses for administering pediatric oral medications, insulin, or emergency allergy shots

facts_and_myths.claim: All medical syringes must use sharp metal needles to dispense medicine.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Many pediatric school syringes are needleless oral dispensers designed to deliver liquid antibiotics or fever reducers smoothly into a child's mouth.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Needleless jet injectors can deliver vaccines through the skin using high-pressure micro-jets of fluid without needles.

facts_and_myths.claim: Syringes operate on atmospheric pressure and the creation of an internal vacuum.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Pulling back the plunger increases barrel volume, lowering internal air pressure so ambient atmospheric pressure forces liquid up into the chamber.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Scottish physician Alexander Wood invented the modern hypodermic syringe and needle in 1853 to alleviate his wife's neuralgic pain.

name: Sterile Saline Eye Drops
visual_anchor: A small squeeze dropper bottle dispensing a single crystal-clear sterile saline droplet poised above an eyewash cup, 9:16 vertical macro view.
core_traits: Sterile isotonic saline liquid formulated to match the salt concentration and pH of natural human tears
Packaged in small squeeze dropper bottles or single-use plastic ampoules
Rinses out dust particles, chalk dust, and chemical splashes from irritated eyes
Provides rapid hydration for dry eyes after long hours of textbook reading or computer screen strain

facts_and_myths.claim: Tap water is just as safe and effective as sterile saline for rinsing out an irritated eye.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Unsterile tap water contains microscopic amoebae such as Acanthamoeba and lacks balanced osmolarity, risking severe corneal infections and tissue swelling.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Isotonic 0.9% saline matches human blood and tear osmolarity, preventing osmotic shock to sensitive corneal cells.

facts_and_myths.claim: Human tears contain a natural antimicrobial enzyme that destroys bacterial cell walls.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Tears contain lysozyme, discovered by Alexander Fleming, which breaks down peptidoglycan bonds in bacterial cell walls within minutes.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Single-dose preservative-free eye drop vials avoid chemical irritants like benzalkonium chloride.

name: Surgical Face Mask
visual_anchor: A three-ply pleated light-blue surgical face mask with white elastic ear loops and moldable nose bridge wire, 9:16 vertical view on a clinic tray.
core_traits: Loose-fitting disposable face covering that covers the mouth and nose
Constructed from three layers of non-woven fabric including a melt-blown polymer electrostatic filter
Secured by soft elastic ear loops and an adjustable bendable metallic nose clip wire
Catches large respiratory droplets emitted by the wearer during coughing, sneezing, or speaking

facts_and_myths.claim: Surgical masks provide airtight hermetic seals that block all airborne viral aerosols equally.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Surgical masks are loose-fitting barrier devices designed for source control against large fluid droplets, unlike tightly sealed N95/FFP2 respirators.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Dr. Wu Lien-teh designed the modern multi-layer cloth plague mask during the Great Manchurian Plague of 1910-1911.

facts_and_myths.claim: The middle layer of a surgical mask uses electrostatic attraction to trap fine particles.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The melt-blown polypropylene layer is given a semi-permanent electric charge (electret) that acts like a microscopic magnet, pulling in airborne particles.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The colored blue or green outer side is hydrophobic to repel splashes, while the soft white inner layer absorbs exhaled moisture.

name: Wooden Underarm Crutches
visual_anchor: A pair of polished blonde wooden axillary crutches with padded rubber underarm cushions leaning against a school nurse's desk, 9:16 vertical perspective.
core_traits: Mobility walking aid featuring a bow-shaped wooden frame with underarm pads and handgrips
Transfers body weight from an injured leg, ankle, or foot directly to the arms and torso
Equipped with non-slip grooved rubber suction tips at the base for hallway floor traction
Height and handgrip position are adjustable using butterfly wing nuts and pre-drilled holes

facts_and_myths.claim: You should rest your entire body weight firmly on the padded underarm tops of the crutches when standing.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Leaning heavily on underarm pads compresses the brachial plexus nerves in the axilla, causing dangerous temporary crutch paralysis in the hands.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Physical therapists teach that all body weight must be supported strictly by the hands and extended arms, leaving 2 inches of clearance under the armpit.

facts_and_myths.claim: Crutches have been used as medical mobility devices for over four thousand years.
facts_and_myths.explanation: An ancient Egyptian carving on the tomb of Kirkor from 2830 BCE depicts a man using a wooden walking crutch with an underarm crossbar.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Modern school crutches are crafted from sturdy laminated birch or hardwood to absorb walking vibrations.

name: Sterile Cotton Swab
visual_anchor: A long wooden applicator stick tipped with a puffy white sterile cotton bud, dipping into antiseptic betadine solution, 9:16 vertical close-up.
core_traits: Slender stick made of wood, rolled paper, or plastic with a tight wad of absorbent cotton spun at one or both ends
Used in school clinics for precise antiseptic application, cleaning wounds, and sampling throat swabs
Absorbs and delivers topical ointments, alcohol, and iodine without touching skin directly
Common tool in science classrooms for cheek cell cheek scraping in microscope labs

facts_and_myths.claim: Doctors recommend using cotton swabs to clean earwax deep out of ear canals.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Inserting cotton swabs into the ear canal pushes earwax deeper against the eardrum, risking impaction, infection, and ruptured tympanic membranes.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Packaging for major cotton swab brands explicitly prints a warning: 'Do not insert inside the ear canal'.

facts_and_myths.claim: Cotton swabs were invented by a father who wrapped cotton around a toothpick to clean his baby.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In 1923, Leo Gerstenzang watched his wife paste cotton to a toothpick to clean their infant and founded the company that created Q-tips.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The 'Q' in Q-tips originally stood for 'Quality'.

name: Instant Chemical Cold Pack
visual_anchor: A flexible white plastic pouch being squeezed firmly to rupture an internal water bag, frosting over with condensation, 9:16 vertical framing.
core_traits: Disposable plastic pouch containing dry ammonium nitrate or urea pellets and an inner fragile bag of water
Activated by squeezing or hitting the pack to rupture the inner water pouch
Triggers an immediate endothermic dissolution reaction that drops temperature to near freezing within seconds
Applied to athletic sprains, bruises, and schoolyard bumps to reduce pain and swelling

facts_and_myths.claim: An instant cold pack gets cold because it releases stored liquid nitrogen gas.
facts_and_myths.explanation: It gets cold through chemical thermodynamics; the dissolution of ammonium nitrate in water is endothermic, absorbing heat directly from the environment.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: No refrigeration is required before activation, making them ideal emergency kits for school sports fields.

facts_and_myths.claim: Applying an ice pack directly to bare skin for an hour without a cloth barrier accelerates tissue recovery.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Applying ice directly to bare skin for prolonged periods can freeze epidermal cells and cause frostbite or tissue necrosis; 15-20 minutes wrapped in cloth is the clinical limit.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Cold causes local vasoconstriction, which limits internal bleeding and edema following a blunt impact injury.

name: School First Aid Kit Box
visual_anchor: A bold white metal wall cabinet emblazoned with an emergency green and white cross, opened to reveal organized bandages, antiseptic bottles, and shears, 9:16 vertical view.
core_traits: Durable wall-mounted metal cabinet or portable plastic toolbox with prominent cross insignia
Houses organized emergency medical supplies for treating playground injuries, burns, and sudden illness
Stocked with adhesive bandages, sterile gauze pads, medical tape, antiseptics, scissors, and tweezers
Mandatory safety installation in school classrooms, science laboratories, and gymnasium offices

facts_and_myths.claim: First aid kits were originally standardized for civilian school classrooms.
facts_and_myths.explanation: First aid kits were developed in 1888 by Johnson & Johnson after railway surgeons needed portable sterile equipment to treat railroad workers injured on remote tracks.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The concept quickly expanded to factories, schools, and homes worldwide.

facts_and_myths.claim: The universal symbol for first aid according to ISO standards is a white cross on a green background.
facts_and_myths.explanation: ISO 7010 designates a white cross on green for medical safety equipment, while the red cross on white is the protected Geneva Convention emblem reserved for wartime military relief.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Commercial companies use green cross or white cross on blue to avoid violating the Red Cross trademark treaty.

name: Acoustic Stethoscope
visual_anchor: A brushed stainless steel dual-head stethoscope chestpiece resting on a white clinic examination desk with flexible navy rubber tubing, 9:16 vertical view.
core_traits: Acoustic medical device for auscultation, or listening to internal sounds of the human body
Features a disc-shaped chestpiece with a flat plastic diaphragm for high frequencies and an open bell for low frequencies
Transmits sound waves through twin flexible rubber air tubes to sealed angled earpieces
Used by school nurses to assess student heartbeats, lung respiratory wheezes, and blood pressure sounds

facts_and_myths.claim: Stethoscopes use electronic microphones to amplify heartbeat sounds.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Acoustic stethoscopes operate entirely on mechanical physics, transmitting pressure sound waves sealed inside hollow air tubes without electronic amplification.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Electronic digital stethoscopes do exist, but traditional acoustic models remain the most widely used by healthcare professionals.

facts_and_myths.claim: The stethoscope was invented by a French doctor who felt uncomfortable placing his ear directly on female patients' chests.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In 1816, Dr. Rene Laennec rolled up a tube of paper to listen to a young woman's heart, discovering that acoustic acoustics transmitted sound louder and clearer.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Laennec carved the first wooden cylindrical stethoscope by hand in Paris.

name: Elastic Compression Bandage
visual_anchor: A tan woven elastic bandage being smoothly wrapped in a figure-eight pattern around a student's sprained ankle, secured with metal clips, 9:16 vertical view.
core_traits: Stretchable woven fabric bandage made of cotton interwoven with elastic rubber or spandex threads
Applies consistent therapeutic compression to support sprained joints and minimize internal swelling
Secured in place using small aluminum teeth clips, safety pins, or self-adhering cohesive coatings
Core component of the standard R.I.C.E. protocol (Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation) for athletic injuries

facts_and_myths.claim: Wrapping an elastic bandage as tightly as possible guarantees the fastest joint healing.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Wrapping too tightly acts like a tourniquet, cutting off arterial blood flow and causing numbness, tingling, cyanosis, and tissue damage.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: If toes or fingers turn pale, cold, or tingle, the elastic bandage must be unwrapped and loosened immediately.

facts_and_myths.claim: The original ACE bandage brand name stands for 'All Cotton Elastic'.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Invented in 1918 by Becton, Dickinson and Company (BD), the acronym ACE stood for 'All Cotton Elastic', highlighting its breathability and washability.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Washing the bandage in warm soapy water restores the elasticity of the rubber threads after stretching.

name: Antiseptic Wound Wipes
visual_anchor: A foil packet torn open to reveal a folded white non-woven antiseptic wipe moist with alcohol, gleaming under 9:16 clinic lighting.
core_traits: Pre-moistened non-woven towelette saturated with antiseptic solutions like isopropyl alcohol or benzalkonium chloride
Individually sealed in sterile, airtight foil packets to prevent evaporation
Gently cleans dirt, bacteria, and debris from intact skin surrounding cuts before dressing
Compact, spill-proof sanitizing essential for field trip travel first aid kits

facts_and_myths.claim: Pouring 70% rubbing alcohol directly into an open bleeding wound is the healthiest way to clean it.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Alcohol and hydrogen peroxide damage healthy living skin cells and slow down healing; antiseptic wipes should clean surrounding skin, while clean water flushes the wound.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Modern school first aid protocols emphasize benzalkonium chloride sting-free wipes over pure alcohol pads for children's scrapes.

facts_and_myths.claim: Alcohol wipes kill bacteria by dissolving their lipid membranes and denaturing proteins.
facts_and_myths.explanation: 70% isopropyl alcohol penetrates bacterial cell walls more effectively than 100% alcohol because water slows evaporation and assists protein denaturation.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Pure 100% alcohol coagulates the outer cell wall too quickly, trapping bacteria in a dormant protective shell.
